3b.text: The study describes Twitter sentiment datasets and a machine learning algorithm used, along with performance measures and gold standard and estimation results. Gold standard results are created by splitting the data into in-sample and out-of-sample datasets. In-sample datasets are created by dividing each language dataset into in-sets of varying lengths (multiples of 10,000 tweets), with the out-set being the subsequent 10,000 tweets. The study then trains sentiment classification models on these in-sets and evaluates their performance on the corresponding out-sets, using measures like Alpha and F1. The results are summarized in tables and visualized in box plots, comparing different estimation procedures. The study aims to analyze these procedures and their performance in approximating the gold standard results.

7b.text: The study describes the creation of Twitter sentiment datasets and employs a machine learning algorithm, specifically a TwoPlaneSVMbin model, to estimate performance. The data is split into in-sample (in-set) and out-of-sample (out-set) datasets, with 138 in-sets and corresponding out-sets created from 13 language datasets. Each in-set is trained, and its performance is measured on the out-set using Alpha and F1 metrics. The goal is to compare different estimation procedures and their accuracy in approximating the out-set gold standard results, with findings presented in various tables and figures.

3b.text: This paper discusses the fine-tuning of a general language model with specific target data to create personalized language models for the short message reply application. The authors propose efficient transfer learning schemes, including freezing certain layers or adding surplus layers, to achieve this. They trained a general language model with literary-style data and applied transfer learning with spoken-style data, demonstrating the model's ability to mimic target user's language style. The experiments showed that the personalized language model learned the target language style properly and outperformed other models in message-reply prediction tasks. The authors used the WMT'14 corpus for initial training and applied transfer learning with data from the "Friends" drama and English bible data. The results indicated that the personalized language model generated outputs closer to the target user's dialogue, with more biblical-like vocabulary and sentence styles when trained with English bible data. The study highlights the effectiveness of transfer learning for personalized language modeling, particularly in scenarios like short message reply applications, while also emphasizing the importance of privacy-preserving techniques.

7b.text: The study proposes transfer learning schemes for personalized language modeling, specifically for RNN-based models with privacy preservation. Experiments involve training a general language model with WMT data and movie script data, then fine-tuning with "Friends" drama scripts and character-specific corpora. Two types of experiments are conducted: sentence completion and message-reply prediction. The model outputs are evaluated qualitatively and quantitatively, showing higher similarity to target user dialogue. The experiments use a general language model trained for 10 days, followed by 4 hours of personalized training, with vocabularies set at 50,002 words. The results indicate proper learning of target language styles, with personalized models generating shorter, more dialogue-like outputs compared to general models. Transfer learning schemes include relearning the whole model, adding surplus layers, and fixing certain layers.

3b.text: This work explores memory-augmented recurrent networks for dialogue coherence, introducing two architectures based on the Neural Turing Machine (NTM). The first design uses a sequence-to-sequence architecture with two separate NTM modules for each participant, while the second design employs a single NTM for both speakers, replacing the sequence-to-sequence architecture with a neural language model. Both models incorporate NTMs to store parallel context information for dialogue coherence. The NTMs update their internal memory at the end of each segment, allowing for context tracking across turns. The second design also uses two NTMs, each for one speaker, to ensure each participant's history is maintained. The NTM-LM system combines the encoder-decoder architecture into a single language model, predicting all utterances in sequence. This system uses a single NTM and processes the dialogue history in segments, with the GRU state used for read and write operations to the NTM. The study evaluates these models using word-level perplexity and compares them to existing baselines, with the NTM-LM system showing promising results.

7b.text: This work explores memory-augmented dialogue systems using Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) to enhance dialogue coherence. Two architectures are introduced: D-NTMS, which uses two NTMs for each speaker, and NTM-LM, which employs a single NTM. Both systems split dialogue into segments, with GRUs processing each segment and writing to the NTM. D-NTMS uses two NTMs to track each speaker's history, while NTM-LM uses one NTM to store context information. The systems are evaluated on the Ubuntu Dialogues Corpus, with perplexity performance reported. The architectures are designed to improve the flexibility and coherence of dialogue responses.

3b.text: This work addresses the issue of unintended bias in abusive language detection models, specifically focusing on gender bias. It highlights the limitations of existing models, which can lead to false positive bias, particularly when they are trained in a supervised learning setting. The authors propose a solution by generating an unbiased test set for each gender using a template method and propose three reduction methods: debiased word embedding, gender swap data augmentation, and fine-tuning with a larger corpus. They also compare the effects of different pre-trained word embeddings and model architectures on gender bias. The work emphasizes the importance of measuring and mitigating unintended bias, as traditional evaluation sets can be biased. The authors use metrics such as AUC scores and equality differences to evaluate the fairness and generalization ability of the models. They demonstrate that their proposed methods can reduce gender biases up to 90-98%, improving the robustness of the models. The authors also discuss the potential for adversarial training methods to further improve bias mitigation while maintaining or even increasing classification performance.

7b.text: Automatic detection of abusive language is crucial for online platforms to prevent personal trauma, cyber-bullying, and hate crimes. However, recent studies have highlighted the robustness and bias issues in machine learning models used for this task. Specifically, models may overfit to neutral words that frequently appear in training data, leading to false positive biases. For instance, "You are a good woman" might be flagged as "sexist" due to the word "woman." This bias is often unmeasurable in standard experiments due to biased validation/test sets. To address this, researchers propose generating an unbiased test set using identity term templates and three reduction methods: debiased word embedding, gender swap data augmentation, and fine-tuning with a larger corpus. These methods aim to mitigate gender biases in abusive language detection models, improving their generalization and robustness. The effectiveness of different pre-trained word embeddings and model architectures is also compared. The proposed methods can reduce gender biases by up to 90-98%, though some classification performance may drop. Future work could explore adversarial training methods to address these issues while maintaining or improving classification performance.

3b.text: Propaganda effectiveness depends on the emotions it elicits, which is challenging to detect due to the complexity of emotions and the need to consider how they affect readers rather than just the text itself. Models like Robert Plutchik's circumplex and 3D models of pleasure, arousal, and dominance have been proposed, but these are complex and not widely used for text analysis. Depechemood, a lexicon-based method, uses a matrix approach to detect emotions in text, derived from crowd-annotated news articles. It categorizes emotions into 8 main subsets and scores words for these categories. The study found that both Catholic and ISIS propaganda materials scored highest in the "inspired" category, with the lowest scores for "afraid." This method also identified different inspiring words in Catholic and ISIS propaganda, with "being afraid" being the lowest score in ISIS material. The method's effectiveness is further illustrated by its consistent high scores for inspiration in ISIS propaganda across multiple articles.

7b.text: Emotion detection in text, particularly for propaganda analysis, faces two main challenges: the complexity of emotions and the difficulty in detecting reader-evoked emotions. The Depechemood model, a lexicon-based approach, categorizes emotions into 8 classes: AFRAID, AMUSED, ANGRY, ANNOYED, DON'T CARE, HAPPY, INSPIRED, and SAD. This model uses crowd-annotated news articles to derive emotion-word matrices. Analysis of Catholic and ISIS-related materials using Depechemood showed that both scored highest in the "inspired" category, with "being afraid" having the lowest score. The method identified different inspiring words in each corpus, and in ISIS propaganda, every issue scored highest in inspiration and lowest in fear.

3b.text: Sentence simplification aims to transform complex sentences into simpler ones, enhancing their interpretability and accessibility for human readers and improving downstream NLP tasks. Recent advancements in neural machine translation have led to the exploration of neural simplification models, such as sequence-to-sequence (Seq2seq) models. This study introduces a memory-augmented RNN architecture called Neural Semantic Encoders (NSE) for sentence simplification. The proposed NseLstm model, using NSE as the encoder and LSTM as the decoder, outperforms other models in terms of both automatic and human evaluation metrics. The model significantly reduces reading difficulty while preserving grammaticality and original meaning, demonstrating effectiveness across various datasets.

7b.text: Sentence simplification aims to make complex sentences easier to interpret and process, benefiting human readers and downstream NLP applications. Recent work has explored neural machine translation (NMT) approaches, with sequence-to-sequence (Seq2seq) models, including LSTM and GRU architectures, showing promise. However, these models often struggle with long-term dependencies. This study proposes using Neural Semantic Encoders (NSE), a memory-augmented RNN architecture, for sentence simplification. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate that the NSELSTM model, which uses NSE as the encoder and LSTM as the decoder, outperforms other models in terms of automatic evaluation measures and human judgments, effectively reducing reading difficulty while preserving grammaticality and meaning.

3b.text: Model overconfidence can lead to poor performance, as it causes the model to concentrate its output on the correct character, preventing it from indicating sensible alternatives. This is evident in the baseline network where the SoftMax function's derivative approaches zero as the model's output becomes concentrated on the correct character. Overconfidence can also harm learning deeper layers and negatively impact beam search, leading to errors such as deletion. To mitigate this, temperature adjustments were made to the SoftMax function, resulting in a more uniform distribution of probabilities. This allowed for the demonstration of the impact of model confidence on beam search without affecting next-step predictions. However, overconfidence can also cause the model to overfit, leading to low accuracy in next-step predictions. Solutions include smoothing techniques like label smoothing, which prevents the model from concentrating all probability mass on a single token, and neighborhood smoothing, which assigns probability mass to neighboring tokens in the transcript. These techniques increase the entropy of predictions, allowing beam search to discover good solutions without the need for temperature control.

7b.text: Model confidence, promoted by cross-entropy training, can lead to overfitting and impact beam search accuracy. By adjusting the SoftMax function's temperature, the character probability distribution can be made more uniform, but the model's preferences remain. Label smoothing, originally proposed for Inception, prevents overconfidence by smoothing the ground-truth label distribution, leading to better gradient flow and reduced model error. Neighborhood smoothing, which assigns remaining probability mass to neighboring tokens, further regularizes the model and improves greedy decoding accuracy. Global normalization, though expensive, can be approximated by locally normalized models with proper regularization like label smoothing. Beam search accuracy can be improved by tuning the SoftMax temperature, but care must be taken to avoid incomplete transcripts.

3b.text: This work proposes an interactive machine translation framework to modernize historical documents, aiming to reduce human effort while maintaining error-free versions. The framework integrates human input with machine learning to overcome the challenges posed by historical language and evolving linguistic norms. Experiments in a simulated environment showed significant reductions in human effort needed to produce modernized versions of historical documents. The study compared two machine translation approaches: Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) and Neural Machine Translation (NMT). Both SMT and NMT improved the modernization quality, but NMT performed poorly for documents like "El Conde Lucanor," where the modernization quality was very low, leading to increased human effort. The interactive framework successfully reduced human effort for documents like the Dutch Bible and "El Quijote," but increased effort for "El Conde Lucanor." SMT consistently achieved the highest effort reduction, aligning with its better modernization quality.

7b.text: This work proposes an interactive machine translation framework for modernizing historical documents, aiming to reduce the human effort needed to produce error-free modern versions. The framework allows scholars to collaborate with machines, addressing the language barrier in historical documents. Modernization, while improving document comprehension, is still prone to errors. The study tested this approach on simulated environments, achieving significant reductions in human effort for modernizing documents like the Dutch Bible and El Quijote. SMT approaches generally yielded better results, reducing the workload by up to 48 points in terms of WSR and 8 in terms of MAR. However, for El Conde Lucanor, both SMT and NMT approaches increased the effort needed due to low modernization quality.

3b.text: The Transformer encoder introduced in BIBREF13 processes an input matrix $H \in \mathbb {R}^{l \times d}$, projecting it through learnable matrices $W_q$, $W_k$, $W_v$ to form query, key, and value vectors. Multi-head self-attention is applied, using $n$ groups of $W_q$, $W_k$, $W_v$ to enhance attention capabilities, with outputs concatenated and processed by a learnable $W_o$ to form the final output. The output of multi-head attention is then passed through position-wise feed-forward networks, which include parameters $W_1$, $W_2$, $b_1$, $b_2$ and hyper-parameter $d_{ff}$. Layer normalization and residual connections are also employed. To address the issue of directionality and distance awareness in self-attention, a modified attention mechanism is introduced, using relative positional encodings $R_{t-j}$ to calculate attention scores and biases. This improvement is based on BIBREF17 and BIBREF19.

7b.text: The Transformer encoder, as introduced in BIBREF13, processes an input matrix \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times d}\) using learnable matrices \(W_q\), \(W_k\), and \(W_v\) to project it into different spaces. Multi-head self-attention, involving several groups of these matrices, enhances the model's ability. The output of multi-head attention is further processed by position-wise feed-forward networks with parameters \(W_1\), \(W_2\), \(b_1\), and \(b_2\). To improve direction- and distance-aware characteristics, relative positional encodings \(R_{t-j}\) are introduced, and the model avoids direct multiplication of learnable parameters by using one parameter instead.

3b.text: Previous work has shown that pretraining an end-to-end model on ASR data from a high-resource language can improve low-resource automatic speech-to-text translation (AST). Factors such as language relatedness and pretraining data size influence performance. This study experiments with pretraining on datasets of varying sizes, including related and unrelated languages to the AST source language. The best predictor of final AST performance is the word error rate of the pretrained ASR model, and differences in ASR/AST performance correlate with how phonetic information is encoded in the later RNN layers. Pretraining and data augmentation yield complementary benefits for AST. The end-to-end system architecture used for both ASR and AST is an encoder-decoder model. Pretraining only the encoder parameters and augmenting the AST data with Kaldi's 3-way speed perturbation were explored. The study found that the encoder accounts for most of the benefits of transferring parameters, and that the Spearman rank correlation of ASR and BLEU scores computed on dev sets is -0.97. Data augmentation improved AST performance, as shown in Table 2.

7b.text: This study explores pretraining automatic speech-to-text (AST) models on automatic speech recognition (ASR) data from high-resource languages to improve performance on low-resource languages. Key findings include that the word error rate (WER) of the pretrained ASR model is the best predictor of final AST performance, and that pretraining and data augmentation yield complementary benefits. The experiments use various ASR datasets, including English, French, and Chinese, and show that pretraining can significantly improve AST performance, with the amount of pretraining data and language relatedness playing significant roles. The end-to-end system architecture, which includes an encoder-decoder model, is consistent across ASR and AST tasks.

3b.text: The narrator, Mr. Madison, arrives in Granite City to investigate a potential insurance fraud at a quarry. He encounters Marshal Thompson, the local marshal, who is skeptical of outsiders. The quarry is in disarray, with blood stains indicating accidents. The foreman, Kelvin, insists the work is done by skilled craftsmen, not just laborers. Madison learns the quarry is part of a larger scheme to defraud Manhattan-Universal Insurance. He meets Professor Parnell, a resident who has been living in the town for over a year, and learns the quarry is part of a yearly extraction process. Parnell reveals he is unable to leave due to the town's refusal to allow him to use the only telephone and mail service. Madison considers the job unsuitable for an investigative adjuster and decides to leave, despite Parnell's reluctance.

7b.text: Marshal Thompson, an insurance agent, investigates a quarry in Granite City, where he finds evidence of unsafe working conditions and potential fraud. The foreman, Kelvin, defends the local stone workers as skilled craftsmen, but Thompson suspects the quarry of defrauding the insurance company. At the local supermarket, Thompson meets Professor Arnold Parnell, a Duke University professor who has been trapped in Granite City for five months due to the town's suspicious behavior and lack of communication. Parnell reveals that the town's residents refuse to cash his traveler's checks and prevent him from leaving, even though he has no physical restraints. Thompson considers the town's actions as part of a larger conspiracy and contemplates leaving with Parnell.

3b.text: American dentistry has transformed from a necessary evil to a lucrative industry, driven by cosmetic treatments and the vanity of aging baby boomers. The decline in cavities and fillings due to fluoride has led to a surplus of dentists, prompting a shift from drill-and-fill to more pleasant and luxurious experiences. Dentists now offer virtual reality, massage therapy, and hot tubs, and have embraced cosmetic procedures like teeth whitening, porcelain caps, and adult orthodontics. However, this has also led to over-treatment and patients resenting what they perceive as unnecessary procedures. The industry's success has raised expectations, making patients resentful of any inconvenience, such as gum surgeries or night guards. Despite the high cost and potential risks, dentists continue to push these treatments, often at the expense of more medically necessary care. The industry's transformation has made dentistry a lucrative business, but at the cost of patient satisfaction and trust.

7b.text: Dentistry has transformed from a necessary evil to a profitable business in the 1990s, despite predictions of its demise. The profession adapted by becoming more patient-friendly, offering cosmetic treatments like teeth whitening and veneers, and leveraging technology like intra-oral cameras. The success of dentistry led to higher expectations among aging baby boomers, who now seek aesthetic improvements over basic care. This shift has created a complex dynamic where dentists must balance medically necessary treatments with patient desires, often using aggressive marketing techniques to maximize profits. Despite the high cost and inconvenience, patients increasingly object to medically advisable treatments like gum surgeries, viewing them as unnecessary. The industry's success has raised expectations, making patients more critical of any perceived inconveniences in dental care.

3b.text: In 1962, strange objects were observed orbiting Earth, initially mistaken for space junk. Russian technicians reported seeing an American automobile and an ancient car orbiting, leading to accusations of sabotage. The U.S. military denied responsibility, and the incident caused confusion among American scientists. At Mount Palpamar, two photographers were fired for making a practical joke. The President established a commission that found three more reports of strange objects, including an old car. The objects were tracked by radar and identified as part of Solomon's Orbit, a phenomenon observed by Solomon, a junkyard owner in Fullerton, California. Solomon used a combination of engine vacuum and exhaust pressure to launch his old cars into orbit, and the radar network around Fullerton tracked their launches. The incident raised concerns about space debris and the potential for sabotage, with the U.S. military denying responsibility and the Russians attributing the sightings to American attempts to ridicule Soviet space efforts.

7b.text: Solomon, an auto-wrecking yard owner in Fullerton, California, launches old cars into space using a unique combination of engine vacuum and exhaust pressure, creating what is called Solomon's Orbit. His actions are detected by a network of radar stations around the town, leading to a national investigation. The Russian space program mistakenly identifies an American automobile as a meteor, causing confusion and prompting a U.S. presidential commission to investigate strange objects in the sky. The commission uncovers reports of sightings and radar detections of old cars orbiting the Earth, leading to a widespread search for their origin.

3b.text: The passage describes the discovery of a metallic city on a desolate planet by three space explorers. The city, described as malignant and geometrically precise, is the only known structure on the planet, which has been uninhabited for millions of years. The explorers, Martin, Wass, and Rodney, cautiously enter the city, noting its strange geometry and the absence of any life. They discover the city is aligned northward and have no wind, suggesting it may have been built to protect against some unknown force. The explorers are trapped within the city and begin to notice strange, distorted similarities to human behavior and evolution, leading to speculation about parallel evolution on the planet. They also observe the city's protective metal bands and speculate it may have been built to shield against a radioactive past.

7b.text: Three space-scouters, Martin, Wass, and Rodney, land on a desolate planet and discover a geometrically precise, sinister city. The city, with its black walls and strict geometry, seems to impose a northward directionality. The men explore the city, finding a metal band surrounding it and noting its low structures. They speculate about the city's inhabitants and the purpose of the metal band, which appears to be impenetrable. As they explore, Rodney experiences a brief, unsettling encounter, and Wass reports that the metal band is a barrier, trapping them inside the city. The men decide to meet in the city center and consider the possibility that the city's isolation is due to past radioactivity.

3b.text: Koroby, a young woman, insists on being taken to a glowing light despite warnings of danger and the impossibility of reaching it. The group initially resists, but she persists, leading them to a demoralized state. Robert, a mysterious stranger, explains he cannot take her back to her world but can help her reach Terra, a faraway land. He claims he has no name and is stranded on Venus, needing to communicate with his people. Koroby, intrigued and skeptical, accepts his help. They encounter a man who offers to build a signal device to communicate with Robert's people. Robert, who has no name, names himself "Robert" and carries Koroby, who is injured and exhausted, to the Stone City. Yasak, a guard, orders Robert to stay in the city while he carries Koroby. As they walk, Yasak speculates about Robert's identity, while Koroby, now in Yasak's house, is tended by a slave and asks for clothing and water.

7b.text: Koroby, on her way to be married, orders the litter bearers to take her to a light she sees, despite warnings of the impossible journey through matted jungle. She insists, and they reluctantly comply. Koroby encounters a stranger who claims to be from a distant world, Terra, and who reads her thoughts. He explains that he is stranded on Venus and needs to reach the nearest city to communicate with his people. Koroby directs him to the Stone City. After a tiring journey, the stranger, Robert, carries Koroby to Yasak's house, where she recovers. Yasak, the local leader, orders Robert to stay with Koroby in the city. Koroby, now in Yasak's house, meets a slave who cares for her, and Robert, who remains distant. Koroby dreams of Robert, hinting at a developing relationship.

3b.text: In March 2015, Hayden Wood and Amit Gudka moved out of their kitchen office to join Second Home, a coworking space in London. They were initially nervous about acceptance, but familiar faces and a strong business plan helped them decide to join. Second Home offers amenities like a meditation room, a restaurant, and a diverse community including venture capitalists, digital strategy agencies, and fashion app developers. Wood and Gudka benefited from recommendations and networking opportunities, such as a workshop from Blue State Digital and a dinner with Neil Turok. Coworking spaces like Second Home signify a company's identity, attracting businesses from various sectors. The rise of coworking spaces is not solely due to corporate downsizing and the growth of startups and gig economy workers, but also because of the cultural claims they make about the meaning and purpose of work.

7b.text: In March 2015, Hayden Wood and Amit Gudka, founders of Bulb, a renewable energy supplier, moved from a kitchen to a coworking space at Second Home in London. They were attracted by the flexibility and potential for networking, with Wood noting some familiar faces on the website. Second Home, co-founded by Rohan Silva, offers a unique aesthetic and a collaborative culture, hosting various businesses, including venture capitalists and tech companies. Coworking spaces like Second Home and WeWork have expanded beyond tech startups to include a diverse range of businesses, driven by corporate downsizing and the growth of freelancers. These spaces now represent a significant portion of the London office market and are seen as a statement of identity for businesses.

3b.text: Herbert Stein's estate, valued at a modest amount due to the death tax, includes his books, poetry, and prose writings, none of which are subject to taxation. His legacy to his family is primarily intangible, encompassing his principles of thrift, loyalty, and appreciation for America. The estate includes his furniture, clothes, and mementos of Richard Nixon, but these are also tax-exempt. The most valuable items are his poetry, prose, and his father's belief in hard work and prudence, which he passed down to his children. His example of loyalty, his support for his friends, and his ability to put personal crises into perspective have left an indelible mark on his children, providing them with a sense of security and resilience. His deep appreciation for his mother, his friends, and his country, as well as his willingness to help others, are qualities that cannot be taxed.

7b.text: The author, whose father was economist Herbert Stein, reflects on the modest estate left to him and his sister after their father's death. Despite his father's frugality and contributions to economics, the estate faced significant estate taxes due to the "death tax." The father's legacy includes his poetry, writings, and personal items, which are not subject to taxation. He also left behind a legacy of principles, including loyalty, appreciation for America, and the importance of hard work and frugality. The father's advice and example, particularly his stance against seeking money for its own sake, have greatly influenced the author's life. His father's close friendships and his ability to provide reassurance during difficult times are also highlighted, emphasizing the intangible but valuable aspects of his father's legacy.

3b.text: In the aftermath of a police encounter, the narrator reflects on his past, recalling comic books, war, and his mother taking him to see Gone with the Wind. He questions his memories, doubting his involvement in a recent incident and realizing he likely saw the film with his mother. The encounter with the police, described as a nightmare, seems to be a figment of his imagination. Feeling persecuted by his false memories, he seeks help, considering professional intervention to prevent him from harming others.

7b.text: The passage describes a man named Hilliard Turner who is mistaken for a troublemaker and beaten by two police officers. Turner, who is experiencing false memories of the past, tries to explain his actions but is unable to convince the officers. The officers confiscate his magazines and beat him. Turner later realizes his memories are unreliable and seeks help from a psychiatrist, driven by a sense of social responsibility.

3b.text: Pashkov, disguised as a businessman, infiltrates the National Hospital to meet with Cuban refugees. He is recognized by the desk clerk and is led to room 615, where he overhears a conversation about a job offer. Pashkov then enters the room and confronts the Cubans, who initially refuse to work with him but eventually agree. Meanwhile, Kolya and Petya use Pashkov's flier to reach the National Hospital, where they find Colonel James, who resembles Pashkov. Pashkov pretends to be Colonel James and convinces the colonel to let him take him to Moscow for an assignment. Zubov, who is also working for Colonel James, attempts to kidnap Pashkov, mistaking him for the colonel. Pashkov manages to escape and is later met by Anastina Bjorklund, who reveals she has been impersonating Pashkov.

7b.text: Pashkov, disguised as Colonel James, visits a hospital in Stockholm where he finds his Cuban friends in room 615. Meanwhile, Kolya and Petya, aided by Zubov, kidnap Colonel James and take him to the hospital. Pashkov, recognizing his doppelgänger, convinces Zubov of the truth and escapes. Colonel James, revealed to be Pashkov, is taken to Petchareff by Zubov. At Petchareff, Pashkov, now back in his original appearance, enjoys a lavish breakfast prepared by nurse Anastina Bjorklund, who questions why he changed his face.

3b.text: The passage describes the crew's preparations for a space mission, with George Randall, the junior crew member, feeling nauseous at the prospect. Captain Brooke assigns the crew to emergency planes, including Tom Bernan, Scotty, and George Randall. Randall is visibly shaken by the mission. After the crew boards the ship, Captain Dennis Brooke, the captain, reveals that the interplanetary liner has been destroyed and no survivors were found. He deduces that Koerber fired the Genton shells that destroyed the ship. Randall, who had been hiding, confesses his intention to help with welding, but his words reveal his fear. Captain Brooke, understanding Randall's fear, accepts his help. The crew, including Dallas, expresses relief at Randall's presence, emphasizing that his presence is crucial for their survival. They prepare to explore the wreckage of Koerber's ship, with Dallas criticizing those who failed to be at their battle stations during the emergency.

7b.text: Captain Dennis Brooke led a boarding party consisting of Tom, Scotty, Dallas, and George Randall to investigate a drifting interplanetary liner, suspecting it was sabotaged by Koerber. Inside, Brooke confirmed the cargo was missing and no survivors remained, leading him to conclude Koerber was responsible. Back on the cruiser, the crew discussed their situation, with Dallas suggesting they might find fuel for their atom-busters. Brooke ordered repairs and exploration, while Dallas criticized Randall for not being at his post. Brooke, though angry, allowed Randall to help with welding, seeing him as a rookie in need of a chance.

3b.text: The Odyssey explores themes of violence and revenge through Odysseus and the suitors. Odysseus, upon returning to Ithaca, encounters a hostile household, including the murderous suitors who have taken over his home. Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, reveals his identity to his loyal slave Eumaeus and his son Telemachus, who are also present. The suitors, led by Eurymachus, mock and taunt Odysseus, leading to a confrontation. Athena, in disguise, calms the suitors and encourages them to leave, but Odysseus remains hidden. The suitors, including Eurymachus, are killed by Odysseus and his allies, with Athena intervening to prevent further bloodshed. Meanwhile, in Mycenae, Agamemnon's son Orestes avenges his father's death by killing his mother Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. Zeus warns of the dangers of human folly, exemplified by Aegisthus. The poem also touches on themes of revenge and the suffering caused by war, as seen in the story of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra.

7b.text: The passages describe various aspects of Homer's *Odyssey*, focusing on the suitors' crimes against Odysseus and his son Telemachus, Odysseus' return to Ithaca, and the subsequent killing of the suitors. The suitors are portrayed as greedy and destructive, consuming Odysseus' property and threatening his family. Odysseus, upon his return, is filled with rage and ultimately kills the suitors, though he experiences guilt over the suffering he caused. The passages also detail Odysseus' interactions with various characters, including Telemachus, Penelope, and his father Laertes, and his eventual victory over the suitors with the help of Athena and Zeus. Specific epithets and similes, such as the suitors being "hyper-" (excessive) and the simile comparing Odysseus' tears to a woman's grief, are used to emphasize the gravity of the situation.

3b.text: Steve Jobs, despite not being particularly interested in mechanical things, was eager to spend time with his father. He discovered a photograph of his father from his time in the Coast Guard, which he found attractive. Jobs felt ashamed when he realized he was smarter than his parents, leading him to admire his father's competence and ability to solve mechanical problems. Unlike his father, Jobs had sweet manners and a self-effacing grace. He was creative and a great student, showing a creative streak in dressing in costume and staying in character. Jobs had no license plate on his Mercedes and often parked in handicapped spaces, which became a running gag. His father, recognizable by his trademark jeans and black turtleneck, was often photographed by curious parents. Jobs' father, Reed Powell, attended his son's high school graduation, which was against all odds, and Jobs refused to have a license plate on his car, viewing it as a way to remain a rebel.

7b.text: Steve Jobs, as described in Walter Isaacson's biography, had a complex relationship with his father, discovering early on that he was smarter than his father, which caused him significant shame.
